name: Brush cut

card.summary: A short, upright haircut with the top the same short length all over, tapered at the sides, that gives a clean, low-maintenance look and makes the head and jaw outline prominent.

quick.overview:
A brush cut keeps the top of the hair short in every dimension, around 6 to 13 mm, following the shape of the head, with the lower sides and back tapered with clippers. It is closely related to the crew cut and flat top.

It matters for looks because very short hair shows off the head and jawline and needs little styling, and an upright front can add a bit of lift at the forehead.
quick.how: It is cut by a barber with clippers and shears, often with the front slightly longer, and traditionally styled with a firm wax. Thick hair that stands up suits it best, and barbers tailor the shape to face and skull shape.
quick.risks: No medical risks. It leaves little hair to hide hairline or scalp features, and thin or very soft hair may not stand up.

lead: The brush cut is a short haircut in which the top is cut to a uniform short length, about 6 to 13 mm, following the head's contour, while the lower sides and back are tapered with clippers as in a crew cut. Cuts shorter than a quarter inch are called burrs.[1]

For appearance, it replaces length with a clean, structured outline, so head shape and jawline read clearly, and the bristle-like top can be graded slightly longer at the front for a small lift at the forehead. People choose it for the neat look and for how little daily styling it needs.[1][2][3]

The style is historically associated with the military and was adopted by subcultures such as punk.[1] Wikipedia's crew-cut article notes that the 'brush cut' name existed in English since at least the mid-1700s, that college rowing teams helped popularise the short cut, and that it was widespread among US college students in the 1920s and 1930s and among veterans after World War II.[2]

paras: The top and upper back and sides are the same length and follow the head, with variants that grade the top slightly longer toward the front or graduate the front hairline for lift.[1] Wikipedia classes the crew cut, flat top, butch and Ivy League cuts as types of buzz cut; the flat top flattens the top into a level plane, and the butch is a short crew cut with a uniform top length.[2][3]

Grokipedia's AI-generated page describes variants such as a standard brush cut with a top of about 3/8 to 1/2 inch, a very short butch version, a longer top that can be brushed forward, fades into the scalp, textured tops, hard parts and flat-top hybrids; it notes that straight to slightly wavy, medium-coarse hair holds the upright shape best and that fine or curly hair often needs matte product.[4]

Wikipedia's crew-cut article says the style was known as the short pompadour or brush cut and was reportedly worn since at least the mid-eighteenth century, with the French calling it a cut 'like a brush' and Germans calling it a Burstenschnitt. The 'crew cut' name most likely comes from rowing crews at Harvard, Yale, Princeton and Cornell, and electric clippers arriving in 1921 made short cuts quicker for barbers.[2]

It was popular on campuses in the 1920s and 1930s, spread through World War II G.I. haircuts, declined as long hair became fashionable from the mid-1960s, and returned in the late 1970s and early 1980s.[2] Wikipedia's brush-cut page cites mid-century barbering textbooks by Thorpe (1967) and Trusty (1971) and Victoria Sherrow's Encyclopedia of Hair (2006) for the cut's definition.[1]

Brush cuts are commonly used in militaries, either as a form of conformity or as a hygiene measure, and punk cultures and other movements have adopted them as a mark of identity and rebellion; Wikipedia cites a 2014 thesis on Australian hardcore punk for the latter.[1] Wikipedia names NFL quarterback Jake Plummer's Air Force-style brush cut in a photo caption.[1] Grokipedia adds that late-1960s London skinheads adopted close cuts in reaction to hippie long hair.[4]

Barbers follow the usual sequence of edging, siding and topping, cutting the top with clippers or shears over a comb or freehand, and choose the final shape according to face shape, skull shape, hairline and the client's preference. Thick hair that stands up suits the cut best.[2] It is traditionally groomed with a firm brush wax.[1] Wikipedia's buzz-cut article says very short cuts can make the face look more defined and are considered suitable for thinning or receding hairlines.[3]

timeline.event: Motorised electric clippers appear; before them, barbers found the short pompadour among the most time-consuming cuts.[2]
Crew and brush cuts become widespread among US college students.[2]
World War II G.I. haircuts spread the cut, and many men keep it as civilians.[2]
Short cuts decline as long hair becomes fashionable.[2]
The crew-cut family returns, with the flat top most popular in the 1980s.[2]
